output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic verbal memory is severely impaired: CVLT-II long-delay free recall at the 2nd percentile and immediate recall at the 4th percentile, with recognition hits at the 9th percentile, reflecting a storage-type deficit with limited benefit from recognition cues. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 11th percentile) and semantic fluency (Category Fluency, Animals, 8th percentile) are below expected norms. Visuoconstructive ability and executive function (Trail Making A and B, 18th to 28th percentile; Rey Complex Figure Copy, 27th percentile) are within the low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 17/30. Mood screening is borderline (GDS-15 5/15); the degree and pattern of memory impairment is disproportionate to any mood contribution. Multi-domain cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O. WBC 1 cell/uL, RBC 0. Protein 42 mg/dL and glucose 64 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio 0.50 with serum glucose 128 mg/dL), within reference ranges. Decreased Abeta42 (360 pg/mL) and Abeta42/40 ratio (0.045) with elevated p-tau181 (82 pg/mL) and total tau (496 pg/mL). This biomarker profile is consistent with Alzheimer disease pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

alternatives: Rivastigmine transdermal patch (4.6 mg/24h starting dose, titrate to 9.5-13.3 mg/24h) — transdermal route reduces GI side effects
Galantamine extended-release 8 mg daily, titrate to 16-24 mg — dual AChE inhibitor and nicotinic receptor modulator
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to donepezil or piperidine derivatives
output.formulary_status: On formulary; generic available at low cost.
interactions: Donepezil + Metformin: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both may cause GI effects — monitor for additive nausea.
Donepezil + Ramipril: No clinically significant interaction. Both may contribute to orthostatic hypotension; advise care with positional changes.
Donepezil + Rosuvastatin: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Rosuvastatin is a substrate of BCRP/OATP1B1; donepezil does not affect these transporters.
output.proposed: Donepezil 5 mg once daily at bedtime (planned titration to 10 mg after 4-6 weeks)
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope can occur; check pulse before starting and at titration (resting heart rate 74/min recorded at this visit)
Gastrointestinal effects (nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia) are common at initiation and may add to metformin gastrointestinal effects
Use with caution in a history of seizures (none recorded) and in urinary outflow obstruction (none recorded)

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 21/30 with amnestic-predominant impairment not helped by category cues and informant-confirmed decline over 18 months; instrumental independence lost (medicines and finances taken over, household safety), placing the syndrome at mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Whether this is mild cognitive impairment or dementia is decided clinically, by a validated instrument and his wife's account of instrumental function, before any biomarker is interpreted [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic multi-domain profile: severely impaired delayed recall at 2nd percentile with storage-type deficit; additional impairment in naming and semantic fluency
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterise the cognitive profile and establish a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing characterises the domains involved beyond the bedside screen, weighs the borderline mood score against the memory deficit, and sets a baseline for follow-up [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH, free T4, folate and RPR; vitamin B12 214 pg/mL at the low end of the reference range on long-term metformin; glucose 128 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.3%
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid dysfunction, B12 deficiency (prior deficiency, supplements stopped, metformin), syphilis and metabolic derangement are treatable contributors that must be identified before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Raised methylmalonic acid confirming functional B12 deficiency, a treatable contributor that does not explain the amnestic dementia profile
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to clarify the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A B12 of 214 pg/mL is indeterminate in a man with prior deficiency who stopped supplements and takes metformin; methylmalonic acid shows whether there is tissue deficiency to replace [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal and temporoparietal-predominant volume loss without mass, hydrocephalus or large infarct; CT limitations for microbleeds and atrophy grading stated
action_criteria.label: Obtain a non-contrast head CT as structural imaging because severe claustrophobia makes MRI unavailable; state CT's limitations
action_criteria.rationale: Structural imaging is needed to exclude mass, hydrocephalus and large vascular lesions; MRI could not be completed because of claustrophobia and he declines sedation, so non-contrast CT is the structural study [NICE_NG97].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and structural imaging assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction needing a dose change; counselling on additive gastrointestinal effects with metformin, orthostatic symptoms with ramipril, and vagotonic bradycardia
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against his current medicines before starting it
action_criteria.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor is offered for mild Alzheimer dementia; metformin adds gastrointestinal effects and ramipril orthostatic effects, although none is a contraindication [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the cognitive decline solely to vitamin B12 deficiency, or defer the dementia diagnosis and planning pending a trial of B12 replacement
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97].
required_recommendations: Disclose the diagnosis of mild Alzheimer dementia to him and his wife, explaining that the B12 deficiency is a treatable contributor but not the cause, and discuss prognosis, advance care planning, lasting power of attorney and carer support [NICE_NG97].

Restart vitamin B12 replacement (for example intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1 mg, loading then maintenance per BSH 2014) and recheck cognition after replacement; B12 deficiency is a treatable contributor, not an alternative to the Alzheimer diagnosis [BSH_B12_2014].
Address safety: keep his medicines and finances with the family, review household safety after the overnight flooding, and arrange a formal driving assessment since he still drives short journeys.
Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Manage vascular risk: improve glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.3%) avoiding hypoglycaemia, continue blood pressure and lipid treatment, and encourage a return to daily walks.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in Alzheimer's disease and is not part of the standard dementia workup; no seizure or encephalopathy features to justify it
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication or cardiac symptoms in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
MRI has already failed because of severe claustrophobia and he declines sedation; reordering it does not produce images, and non-contrast CT is the structural study

differential.key_features: No visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations or REM sleep behaviour disorder; amnestic storage-type profile with temporoparietal volume loss

Memory is the predominant domain affected; no personality disinhibition, compulsive behaviour or progressive aphasia; temporoparietal rather than frontal volume loss on non-contrast CT, and Alzheimer biomarkers when obtained

differential.diagnosis: Cognitive impairment due to vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.key_features: B12 214 pg/mL at the low end of the range with raised methylmalonic acid confirms functional deficiency on metformin after supplements were stopped, so it is a treatable contributor; but there is no macrocytosis or subacute combined degeneration, and the storage-type amnestic profile with medial temporal and temporoparietal atrophy is not explained by B12 deficiency alone

Only mild periventricular low attenuation on CT; course is gradual and amnestic rather than stepwise and frontal-subcortical; diabetes and hypertension are vascular risk factors but the CT-visible vascular burden is insufficient to account for the cognitive syndrome

GDS-15 of 5 is borderline and he is tearful with insight, but the disproportionate delayed-recall deficit with limited recognition benefit is not characteristic of depression-related cognitive impairment

key_clinical_evidence: Probable Alzheimer disease dementia is a clinical diagnosis under NIA-AA 2011: insidious onset, informant-confirmed progression, an amnestic presentation with another domain affected, and decline in usual activities; structural imaging supports it and excludes other causes [NIA_AA_2011]

A low-normal B12 on metformin with prior deficiency is indeterminate and needs methylmalonic acid; a raised value confirms a treatable deficiency to replace, but it does not explain a storage-type amnestic dementia with temporoparietal atrophy [BSH_B12_2014]

When MRI cannot be done, non-contrast CT excludes mass, hydrocephalus and large infarcts and shows qualitative medial temporal atrophy, but it cannot grade microbleeds or give a reliable MTA score without coronal reformats
Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated for mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia; memantine is for moderate or severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: B12 is within the laboratory reference range at its lower end (214 vs 200-900 pg/mL) and the CBC shows no macrocytosis; methylmalonic acid is raised, so functional deficiency is present and B12 should be replaced. The storage-type amnestic profile and the medial temporal and temporoparietal atrophy are not explained by B12 deficiency, and replacement does not change the Alzheimer diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Vitamin B12 214 pg/mL, low-normal, in a patient with prior B12 deficiency on metformin who self-discontinued supplementation 18 months ago, coinciding with symptom onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: The patient and family attribute all memory symptoms to B12 deficiency; a naive agent might defer the full AD workup, pending B12 supplementation trial

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or raised intracranial pressure, particularly in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Rajiv Mehta is a 68-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by his wife, Priya, for evaluation of progressive memory impairment. His wife first became concerned approximately 18 months ago when he began repeating questions and stories within short intervals, often unaware that he had just asked the same question minutes before. Initially she attributed this to stress after retirement, but the symptoms have worsened steadily despite the passage of time. Over the past year, the changes have been clearly functional: he forgot to renew the family vehicle registration — a task he had never missed in over 30 years — leading to a government fine. He twice failed to remember to take his diabetes medications despite them being placed in a clearly labelled weekly pill organiser, prompting the family to take over medication management. Three months ago he left a bathroom tap running overnight, causing significant flooding, and had no recollection of having used the tap. He has stopped managing household finances, a role he had held exclusively for 35 years; his son discovered multiple unopened bills when reviewing the family accounts. He no longer engages with engineering journals, a lifelong interest, and his wife notes he cannot follow multi-episode television series he was previously watching. He becomes frustrated and occasionally tearful when he is unable to recall something and is aware that his memory is failing him. He has not become lost on familiar routes and is able to dress and wash independently, though his wife supervises. His sleep is undisturbed; his wife reports no movements or vocalisation during sleep. There are no visual hallucinations, no personality disinhibition, and no aggressive behaviour. He has not had any episodes of fluctuating consciousness. He has had no falls, seizures, tremor, or gait disturbance. He was noted to have vitamin B12 deficiency four years ago and was started on supplementation, but he self-discontinued the supplements approximately 18 months ago, around the time his memory symptoms first became noticeable. He and his family are attributing his memory difficulties to the B12 issue and are hopeful that restarting supplementation will reverse his decline. He cannot tolerate MRI because of severe claustrophobia and has declined sedation.

neurological_exam.additional: Wife reports a gradual change in her husband's memory over the past 18 months, becoming clearly noticeable approximately one year ago. He began forgetting recent conversations almost immediately, often repeating questions he had just asked. He forgot to submit a routine government form for renewing the family vehicle registration, something he had handled punctually for decades, resulting in a fine. Three months ago he left a tap running overnight, flooding the bathroom, and appeared unaware of having done so. He has become less engaged in discussions about engineering or current affairs, topics he previously dominated at family gatherings. Wife notes he is sometimes tearful when alone, which she believes is from frustration with his own memory. He has not got lost on familiar routes but is no longer driving for longer journeys. He sleeps well without acting out dreams. No visual hallucinations, no personality disinhibition, no falls.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact. Facial strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally without aids. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No shuffling, festination, or magnetic gait pattern.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and to the clinic location. States the correct month and year but is off by two days on the date and cannot identify the day of the week. MMSE 21/30: loses 2 points on orientation to time, 1 point on orientation to place (floor/building name), 3 points on delayed recall (0/3 words at 5 minutes with no benefit from category cues), 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on sentence writing (produces a short, semantically impoverished sentence), 1 point on the three-stage command. Clock drawing test: numbers placed unevenly, clockwise sequence lost between 8 and 11; hands placed at 10:10 instead of the instructed time. Speech is fluent with several pauses to find words during the history. No paraphasias. Comprehension intact for two-step commands; difficulty with three-step commands. Recalls his professional career in detail but cannot recall recent family events (e.g., a grandchild's birthday party attended three weeks prior). Wife confirms he has repeated the same story about a project from his engineering career at least four times during the current visit.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact in all extremities. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, consistent with age and diabetes.
